title: Consent for colonoscopy in a 25-year-old with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss
desc: In this station the candidate sees a 25-year-old accountant in a hospital pre-admission clinic. His GP has referred him for colonoscopy after 2 years of intermittent diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain, mouth ulcers and unintentional weight loss. The candidate takes a focused pre-procedure history, does a focused examination, then explains the colonoscopy and gains consent using IPBRAD (indication, procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives, documentation). In Part 2 the candidate interprets his pre-admission bloods, stool tests and the colonoscopy and histology report, recognises ileocolonic Crohn's disease, and plans induction treatment, staging, pre-immunosuppression screening and follow-up.
focus: Explaining a colonoscopy and gaining informed consent, then interpreting the results of a suspected Crohn's disease work-up
stem:
You are a gastroenterology resident medical officer (RMO) in the pre-admission clinic of a metropolitan tertiary hospital.

Samuel Brennan, a 25-year-old accountant, has been referred by his GP for a colonoscopy. He has had intermittent diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain, mouth ulcers and unintentional weight loss for 2 years. He is booked for the procedure. You are seeing him today to assess him, explain the colonoscopy and obtain his consent.
tasks: Take a focused history from Samuel, including what he already knows and his fitness for the procedure. Perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Then explain the colonoscopy to him and obtain his consent (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Samuel's pre-admission blood tests, his stool tests and his colonoscopy and histology report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Samuel Brennan, a 25-year-old accountant. You are friendly and cooperative but more nervous than you let on. You have never had a colonoscopy. If the candidate uses jargon (for example "sedation", "perforation", "biopsy" or "polypectomy") without explaining it, ask: "Sorry, what does that mean?" The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Hi. My GP says I need a camera test of my bowel, but I'm not really sure what's involved."

What you know already (give when asked): "It's a camera up the bottom, isn't it? A mate had one and said the drink you have the day before was the worst part." You want to know whether it hurts, whether you will be awake, and how much time you will need off work. You have never had one.

Your symptoms (give only when asked):

  • This started about 2 years ago. Bad patches come every few months and last 2 to 3 weeks.
  • In a bad patch you have 4 to 6 loose, watery stools a day, and sometimes you wake at night to go. There is no blood in your stool.
  • You get crampy pain in your lower right tummy, worse after meals and eased by opening your bowels.
  • You get painful mouth ulcers during the bad patches.
  • You have lost about 6 kg over 6 months (70 kg down to 64 kg) without trying, and you feel tired.
  • Right now you are in a mild patch: 3 to 4 loose stools a day, no blood. You are eating and drinking normally.

Say no to all of these if asked: fever, sweats, vomiting, a swollen tummy, not passing wind, severe pain. Pain, discharge or swelling around your bottom; if asked about lumps there: "There's a little soft bit of skin there. It doesn't hurt." Joint pain or swelling, red or painful eyes, rashes or painful lumps on your shins, yellow skin.

Infection and travel (only if asked): born in Australia. No travel overseas in the last 3 years. Nobody around you has been unwell. No contact with anyone with tuberculosis (TB).

Past medical history: wisdom teeth out under a general anaesthetic at 19, with no problems. No heart or lung problems, no asthma, no diabetes. You don't snore and have not been told you stop breathing in your sleep. No bleeding or bruising problems. No loose teeth, caps or dentures.

Medications:

  • Iron tablets (Ferro-Grad) once a day, started by your GP 3 weeks ago because your iron was low.
  • Loperamide (Gastro-Stop) sometimes on workdays.
  • No blood thinners, aspirin, anti-inflammatories (Nurofen, Voltaren) or herbal medicines.

Allergies: none, including to medicines and latex.

Family history: your mum's sister has "Crohn's or colitis, something like that". No one in the family has had bowel cancer.

Social history:

  • You live with your partner, Jess. Only if asked who could take you home: "Jess could, and she could stay with me that night."
  • You smoke about 10 cigarettes a day and have done for 7 years.
  • Alcohol: 6 to 8 drinks on weekends. No recreational drugs.
  • You are an accountant. It is a busy time at work and you are worried about taking time off.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I wondered about a food intolerance. My GP mentioned something called Crohn's, like my aunt."
  • Concerns: that it will hurt or you will be awake for it. You are also quietly worried it could be cancer because of the weight loss. Say this only if the candidate asks what worries you most.
  • Expectation: you want an answer and something that fixes it.

Questions to raise during the explanation (once each):

  • "Will I be awake for it?"
  • "Can I just drive myself home afterwards? I don't want to bother Jess."

If the explanation has been clear and you have been given the chance to ask questions, agree to go ahead and say you will sign the form.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: thin young man, comfortable, mildly pale. Weight 64 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 20.2.
  • Observations: HR 84 regular, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C.
  • Hands: no clubbing or koilonychia. Mild palmar pallor.
  • Eyes: mild conjunctival pallor. No redness. No scleral icterus.
  • Mouth: two small, shallow aphthous ulcers on the inner lower lip and buccal mucosa.
  • Airway (for sedation): good mouth opening, full dentition with no loose teeth, Mallampati class I, full neck movement.
  • Skin and joints: no erythema nodosum or pyoderma. No joint swelling.
  • Heart and chest: heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft, with mild tenderness in the right iliac fossa. No guarding or rebound. No palpable mass. No hepatosplenomegaly. Bowel sounds normal. Hernial orifices clear.
  • Perianal inspection (if offered, with a chaperone): one small, soft, non-tender perianal skin tag. No fistula opening, abscess or fissure.
  • Digital rectal examination: if requested, say it will be done at the start of the colonoscopy.

check.x: Professionalism

Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Samuel's identity (full name and date of birth) and explains the purpose of the visit: to talk through the colonoscopy and obtain his consent.
Uses plain language without jargon, checks understanding throughout (for example by asking him to explain it back), may use a simple diagram, and acknowledges his anxiety.
History
Before explaining, asks what he already knows about colonoscopy, what he wants to know, and about any previous procedures or sedation.

Confirms weight loss and nocturnal stools, and screens for features that make colonoscopy unsafe now or need urgent care: fever, severe or bloody diarrhoea (a severe flare), severe pain, vomiting, distension or not passing wind (obstruction or perforation).
check.d: Credit if the candidate screens for these or names the contraindications (suspected perforation, fulminant colitis, acute diverticulitis, unable to tolerate sedation) and confirms none applies.

check.x: Assesses fitness for sedation: previous anaesthetic (wisdom teeth, no problems), heart or lung disease, snoring or sleep apnoea, loose teeth, and bleeding problems.

Takes a medication and allergy history: specifically asks about anticoagulants, antiplatelets and NSAIDs (none); identifies the oral iron started 3 weeks ago and the occasional loperamide; no allergies.
Takes a social history: smokes 10 cigarettes a day, drinks 6 to 8 drinks on weekends, is an accountant, and lives with Jess, who can take him home and stay overnight.
Asks about his ideas, concerns and expectations and draws out his main worry (cancer).
Examination
Asks for observations, weight and height (normal observations, BMI 20.2 after the weight loss) and assesses the airway for sedation (mouth opening, dentition, Mallampati class, neck movement).
check.d: The examiner gives the observations, weight and BMI on request.

check.x: Inspects for pallor and looks for extraintestinal signs, finding the aphthous mouth ulcers.
Examines the abdomen: finds mild right iliac fossa tenderness with no mass, guarding, rebound or distension, and normal bowel sounds.
Offers a perianal inspection with a chaperone and is told of a skin tag, with no fistula, abscess or fissure.
Explanation and consent (Part 1)

Explains what a colonoscopy is and why he needs it: a thin, flexible tube with a camera passed through the back passage to look at the large bowel and the end of the small bowel. For Samuel, it looks for the inflammation of Crohn's disease, takes samples and guides treatment.
Explains the preparation:

kids.x: Stop the iron tablets 5 to 7 days before, and stop loperamide (Gastro-Stop) a few days before the prep, as the unit instructs. Blood thinners, if he were on them, would be managed according to the unit's instructions.
Low-fibre diet for 2 to 3 days, then clear fluids the day before. Bowel prep causes frequent watery stools, so he should stay near a toilet and keep drinking.
kids.d: Accept a split-dose prep (evening before and morning of).

kids.x: Fast before the sedation as the unit instructs (no food for about 6 hours; clear fluids only until the cut-off), because sedation needs an empty stomach.

check.x: Explains the procedure itself: a day procedure of about 20 to 30 minutes, lying on his side, under sedation through a drip, usually given by an anaesthetist; most people are asleep or very drowsy and do not remember it, though it is not a full general anaesthetic. The doctor looks for inflammation, ulcers, polyps and bleeding, takes painless biopsies and removes any polyps.
check.d: This answers his question "Will I be awake for it?"

check.x: Explains recovery:

kids.x: Home a few hours later, the same day. He is told the initial findings on the day, and biopsy results come at follow-up. Usually 1 day off work (the prep day may also be disruptive); back to normal activities the next day.

For 24 hours after sedation: no driving, operating machinery, alcohol or important decisions or signing legal documents. A responsible adult must take him home and should stay overnight. Answers his question about driving himself: he cannot.

check.x: Explains the benefit: a definite diagnosis from direct views and biopsies, so the right treatment can start early.
Explains the risks:

kids.x: Common: bloating, cramps and discomfort passing stool for a while; reactions to the bowel prep (nausea, dehydration); reactions to sedation.

Uncommon but serious, with approximate figures: perforation about 1 in 1,000 to 3,000 (higher with polyp removal or severe inflammation), which may need surgery; bleeding about 1 in 100 to 1,000 after polyp removal; infection; missed lesions possible.
Risk of not having it: Crohn's disease could be missed and progress to complications (narrowing, fistulas, malnutrition).

check.x: Names at least two alternatives (e.g. CT or MR enterography, capsule endoscopy, flexible sigmoidoscopy) and explains why colonoscopy is preferred (the only test that sees and biopsies the whole colon and terminal ileum).

Completes consent properly: invites questions, confirms he has understood and agrees freely, tells him he can change his mind, gives written information, and documents consent with his signature on the form.

After the colonoscopy: tells him to contact the unit or go to the ED for severe or worsening tummy pain, a swollen or hard tummy, fever, more than a small amount of bleeding from the bottom, or vomiting in the days after the procedure.
check.d: Credit in Part 1 as part of the explanation of recovery.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the bloods: iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 118, MCV 76, ferritin 16, TSAT 8%), with low ferritin despite inflammation confirming true deficiency; CRP 28, platelets 448 and albumin 31 as active inflammation; negative tTG-IgA with normal IgA makes coeliac disease unlikely.
Interprets the stool tests: calprotectin 520 means intestinal inflammation (against IBS); no enteric pathogens and no C. difficile (against infection).

Interprets the colonoscopy: deep linear ulcers and cobblestoning in the terminal ileum, a narrowed but passable ileocaecal valve, patchy aphthous ulcers in the caecum and ascending colon with normal mucosa between (skip lesions), and a normal rectum (rectal sparing).
Interprets the histology: chronic active ileitis with a non-caseating granuloma, no dysplasia or malignancy, and no acid-fast bacilli.
States the diagnosis as ileocolonic Crohn's disease and links it to his crampy pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and weight loss.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against: ulcerative colitis, coeliac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal TB or infective ileitis, colorectal cancer or lymphoma.
check.d: Award for any three with a specific feature from Samuel's case.

check.x: Management
Arranges staging: MR enterography to map the small bowel and assess the ileocaecal narrowing.

Plans induction with the gastroenterologist: budesonide 9 mg orally daily for about 8 weeks then taper (mild to moderate ileocaecal disease), or prednisolone (e.g. 40 mg orally daily, tapering over about 8 weeks) for more severe disease, with calcium and vitamin D while on prednisolone. Does not use mesalazine for induction.
check.d: Accept prednisolone as reasonable given CRP 28, albumin 31, deep ulcers and weight loss. A remark that aminosalicylates have little role in Crohn's disease is a bonus and is not required. Award for a correctly dosed oral corticosteroid (budesonide 9 mg daily or prednisolone about 40 mg daily with a taper) and no mesalazine for induction. Calcium and vitamin D with prednisolone is expected but does not on its own decide the item.

check.x: Before immunosuppression, screens for at least hepatitis B and latent TB (IGRA and chest X-ray), and lists hepatitis C, HIV, varicella immunity and vaccinations; no live vaccines once immunosuppressed.
check.d: Award for hepatitis B and TB plus any two others.

check.x: Plans steroid-sparing maintenance: a thiopurine after TPMT testing, or methotrexate, escalating to biologic therapy within PBS criteria or earlier through specialist pathways given high-risk features.
check.d: Mentioning NUDT15 testing alongside TPMT is a bonus and is not required.

check.x: Treats the iron deficiency: IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred while the disease is active, with repeat iron studies and FBC.
Strongly advises stopping smoking, explaining that smoking worsens Crohn's disease (more flares and surgery), and offers support (Quitline, pharmacotherapy).
Safety netting

Explains the diagnosis in plain words: long-term inflammation of the gut, here the end of the small bowel and the start of the large bowel. It is not cancer. It is lifelong, with flares and quiet periods, and most people are controlled with medicines; some need surgery over time, especially for narrowing.
check.d: Credit from the explanation given directly to Samuel in the last Part 2 question, including honest answers to his two questions.

check.x: For Crohn's disease: tells him to go to the ED or call the IBD nurse the same day for severe pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy or not passing wind (a blockage); fever; frequent or bloody diarrhoea; feeling faint or dehydrated; or a painful swelling near the bottom. On steroids or immunosuppressants, fever or signs of infection also need prompt review.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, with where to go.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: IBD clinic review in about 4 weeks (response to induction, screening results, starting maintenance), repeat bloods and calprotectin, the IBD nurse's contact, a letter to the GP and written information.
check.d: Award for an IBD clinic review with a timeframe plus any two of: repeat bloods and calprotectin, IBD nurse contact, GP letter, written information.

part2.lead: Samuel had his colonoscopy 10 days after your pre-admission visit and is back in the gastroenterology clinic today for the results. Today he has 3 to 4 loose stools a day without blood, no vomiting or distension, and he is eating. Observations are normal (HR 82, BP 120/74, temperature 36.7 °C). Weight 64 kg. He was born in Australia, has not travelled overseas in 3 years and has no known TB contact. His maternal aunt may have inflammatory bowel disease, and there is no family history of bowel cancer. Here are his pre-admission blood tests, the stool tests his GP sent before referral, and his colonoscopy and histology report.
part2.patient:
Questions 1 to 3 are answered to the examiner. For Question 4 you join the candidate, who speaks to you directly. Ask these once each while the candidate explains the diagnosis and what happens next:

  • "Is this something I'll have for the rest of my life?"
  • "Will I need an operation?"

You are relieved it is not cancer, but daunted by the idea of a lifelong condition. If the candidate uses jargon such as "granulomas", "biologic" or "immunosuppression" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests (pre-admission clinic)
handover.result: Collected at the pre-admission clinic visit. Patient taking oral iron for 3 weeks. Gluten-containing diet.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 118 with MCV 76, ferritin 16 and transferrin saturation 8%: microcytic iron deficiency anaemia. CRP 28, platelets 448 and albumin 31: active inflammation. Normal electrolytes, creatinine, liver enzymes and B12. tTG-IgA negative with a normal total IgA.
  • For Samuel: ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a ferritin of 16 despite active inflammation means true iron deficiency, from chronic mucosal blood loss, reduced intake and inflammation-driven (hepcidin-mediated) reduced iron absorption. The low albumin reflects inflammation and weight loss. Negative coeliac serology on a gluten diet, with a valid IgA level, makes coeliac disease unlikely. A normal B12 is worth noting with terminal ileal disease.
  • What it changes: IV iron is preferred while the disease is active. The inflammatory markers are a baseline to track the response to treatment. Normal renal and liver function are a baseline before thiopurine or biologic therapy.

handover.label: Stool tests (sent by the GP before referral)
handover.result: Stool sample collected by the GP 5 weeks ago, during a flare.
handover.model:
• Read: faecal calprotectin 520 µg/g, about ten times the upper limit. Multiplex PCR for enteric pathogens and C. difficile toxin gene are not detected.
  • For Samuel: a high calprotectin means neutrophilic inflammation of the bowel wall, which argues strongly against irritable bowel syndrome. With no pathogens (including Yersinia, which can cause ileitis) and no C. difficile, infection is unlikely to explain the picture. Calprotectin is not specific: infection, NSAIDs and cancer can raise it too, which is why he needed colonoscopy.
  • What it changes: it justified the colonoscopy, and repeat calprotectin can track his response to treatment non-invasively.

rows.t: Enteric pathogen multiplex PCR (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, STEC, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba histolytica)

handover.label: Colonoscopy and histology report
handover.result:
Procedure: ileocolonoscopy, day procedure, under propofol sedation given by an anaesthetist.

Clinical details: 25-year-old man with 2 years of intermittent diarrhoea, crampy right-sided abdominal pain, mouth ulcers and 6 kg weight loss. Iron deficiency. Raised faecal calprotectin.

Bowel preparation: adequate (Boston Bowel Preparation Scale 8/9). Caecum reached and confirmed by the appendiceal orifice and ileocaecal valve. Terminal ileum intubated for 10 cm.

Findings:

  • Terminal ileum: erythematous, oedematous mucosa over the distal 10 cm with deep linear (longitudinal) ulcers and a cobblestone appearance.
  • Ileocaecal valve: ulcerated and mildly narrowed. The scope passed without resistance.
  • Caecum and ascending colon: patchy small aphthous ulcers separated by normal-appearing mucosa.
  • Transverse, descending and sigmoid colon: normal.
  • Rectum: normal mucosa. Normal retroflexed view.
  • No polyps or masses. No active bleeding.

Representative image of the terminal ileum attached.

Biopsies: terminal ileum, caecum and ascending colon, and segmental biopsies from the transverse, left colon and rectum.

Histology:

  • Terminal ileum: chronic active ileitis with villous blunting, crypt architectural distortion, crypt abscesses and a non-caseating epithelioid granuloma. No acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen stain. No dysplasia or malignancy.
  • Caecum and ascending colon: patchy focal active colitis (focal cryptitis) with intervening normal mucosa.
  • Transverse colon, left colon and rectum: normal colonic mucosa.

Conclusion: active ileitis with a mildly narrowed ileocaecal valve and patchy right-sided colitis with rectal sparing. Chronic active inflammation with a non-caseating granuloma on histology. No dysplasia or malignancy. Clinicopathological correlation recommended.

No immediate complications. Preliminary findings discussed with the patient in recovery.
handover.model:
• Read: the terminal ileum has deep linear ulcers and cobblestoning, the ileocaecal valve is ulcerated and mildly narrowed, the caecum and ascending colon have patchy aphthous ulcers with normal mucosa between them (skip lesions), and the rectum is spared. Histology shows chronic active ileitis (architectural distortion means chronicity), a non-caseating granuloma, no acid-fast bacilli and no dysplasia.
  • For Samuel: ileocolonic Crohn's disease, which explains his crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers, weight loss and iron deficiency; his perianal skin tag also supports Crohn's disease. Against ulcerative colitis: ileal disease, skip lesions, rectal sparing and granulomas. Against intestinal TB: non-caseating granuloma, no acid-fast bacilli and no risk factors (born in Australia, no travel, no TB contact). Against cancer: no mass or dysplasia.
  • What it changes: he needs induction therapy and staging. MR enterography maps the small bowel and assesses the narrowing. Deep ulcers, young age and a narrowed valve are high-risk features that favour early steroid-sparing or advanced therapy (within PBS criteria), so pre-immunosuppression screening should start now.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Samuel Brennan, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Samuel now, here in the gastroenterology clinic.
Samuel joins you. Explain his diagnosis to him and tell him what happens next and when to seek help.
expect:
• Identify: self, gastroenterology RMO, clinic; Samuel Brennan, 25.
  • Situation: colonoscopy results confirm active ileocolonic Crohn's disease; he needs a treatment plan.
  • Background: 2 years of intermittent diarrhoea, crampy right iliac fossa pain, mouth ulcers, 6 kg weight loss; smokes 10 a day; aunt with possible IBD; on oral iron.
  • Assessment: deep linear ulcers and cobblestoning in the terminal ileum, narrowed ileocaecal valve, skip lesions in the right colon, rectal sparing; non-caseating granuloma, no dysplasia. Calprotectin 520, CRP 28, albumin 31, platelets 448. Iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 118, ferritin 16). Stool pathogens, C. difficile and coeliac serology negative. Clinically stable, no obstruction.
  • Recommendation: review today to agree induction therapy, MR enterography, pre-immunosuppression screening, IV iron, IBD nurse, clinic in 4 weeks.

Most likely: ileocolonic Crohn's disease. Crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and weight loss, and a perianal skin tag; terminal ileal linear ulcers and cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing; non-caseating granuloma; raised calprotectin and CRP.

  • Ulcerative colitis: for: chronic diarrhoea, raised calprotectin. Against: ileal disease, skip lesions, rectal sparing, granulomas, no blood.
  • Coeliac disease: for: diarrhoea, weight loss, iron deficiency, mouth ulcers. Against: negative tTG-IgA with normal IgA.
  • Irritable bowel syndrome: for: 2 years of intermittent cramps and diarrhoea. Against: weight loss, nocturnal stools, calprotectin 520, ulcers at colonoscopy.
  • Intestinal TB or infective ileitis: for: ileocaecal disease. Against: no risk factors, non-caseating granuloma, no acid-fast bacilli, negative stool PCR.

1. Induction with the gastroenterologist: budesonide 9 mg orally daily for about 8 weeks then taper (mild to moderate ileocaecal disease), or prednisolone (e.g. 40 mg orally daily, tapering over about 8 weeks) for more severe disease, with calcium and vitamin D while on prednisolone. Not mesalazine for induction.
  2. Staging: MR enterography for small bowel extent and the narrowing.
  3. Screen before immunosuppression: hepatitis B and C, HIV, latent TB (IGRA, chest X-ray), varicella; update non-live vaccines.
  4. Maintenance: thiopurine (after TPMT) or methotrexate; early biologic discussion given high-risk features.
  5. IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose).
  6. Stop smoking: it worsens Crohn's; offer Quitline and pharmacotherapy.

• Explain in plain words: Crohn's disease, long-term inflammation of the end of the small bowel and start of the large bowel; not cancer; lifelong with flares and quiet spells; most people are controlled with medicines; some need surgery, mainly for narrowing.
  • ED or IBD nurse the same day for: severe pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy or not passing wind (a blockage); fever; frequent or bloody diarrhoea; feeling faint or dehydrated; a painful swelling near the bottom.
  • On steroids or immunosuppressants, fever or infection needs prompt review. Do not stop steroids suddenly; avoid anti-inflammatories.
  • Follow-up: IBD clinic in about 4 weeks; MR enterography booked; repeat FBC, iron studies, CRP and calprotectin; IBD nurse contact; GP letter; written information.

ddx.for: Crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and 6 kg weight loss, with terminal ileal linear ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing and a non-caseating granuloma.
Chronic diarrhoea with a raised calprotectin and an aunt with possible IBD.
ddx.against: No rectal bleeding, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions, a normal rectum and granulomas on histology.

ddx.for: Diarrhoea, weight loss, iron deficiency and mouth ulcers.
ddx.against: Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA on a gluten-containing diet.

ddx.for: Two years of intermittent crampy pain and diarrhoea eased by opening his bowels, in a stressed young professional.
ddx.against: Weight loss, nocturnal stools, iron deficiency, calprotectin 520 and ulceration at colonoscopy.

ddx.dx: Intestinal tuberculosis or infective ileitis (such as Yersinia)
ddx.against: Born in Australia with no travel or TB contact, non-caseating granuloma with no acid-fast bacilli, and a negative stool pathogen PCR.

ddx.dx: Colorectal cancer or small bowel lymphoma
ddx.for: Unintentional weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia.
ddx.against: Aged 25, no palpable mass, no mass at colonoscopy and no dysplasia or malignancy on biopsy.

guide:
This is a clinic station, so there is no observation chart. Give the observations, weight and BMI from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them, and give each examination finding only when the candidate says what they are examining.

Part 1 has three parts in 10 minutes: a brief focused history (about 2.5 minutes), a brief focused examination (about 2 minutes) and the explanation and consent (about 5 minutes). The referral already gives the symptoms, so the history only needs to confirm them. If the candidate has not started the examination by about 4 minutes, you may say "Please move on." Credit the consent items (indication, preparation, procedure, recovery, benefits, risks, alternatives, documentation) whenever they come up in Part 1. Samuel raises his two questions (being awake, driving himself home) during the explanation. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the pre-admission bloods are being collected and the results will come in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead (it gives his current state, travel, TB contact and family history), hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. The candidate answers Questions 1 to 3 to you. For Question 4, Samuel joins and the candidate speaks to him directly; Samuel asks his two questions once each during this explanation. Credit the plain-language explanation of the diagnosis, the red flags and the follow-up from this answer. The endoscopy image (linear ulcers and cobblestoning) is marked under Interpretation.

A high-performing candidate finds out what Samuel knows first, screens for features that make the procedure unsafe and for sedation risk, and picks up the oral iron and loperamide. They examine for extraintestinal and abdominal signs and give a structured, jargon-free IPBRAD explanation. That explanation covers stopping the iron and loperamide, the bowel prep, fasting before sedation, honest wording about sedation, no driving for 24 hours, perforation and bleeding with approximate figures, the risk of not having the test and the alternatives, and it ends with documented consent and written information. In Part 2 they read the skip lesions, rectal sparing and granuloma as Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis or TB, interpret the iron deficiency correctly, and plan induction, staging, pre-immunosuppression screening, IV iron, smoking cessation and specific red flags.

A borderline candidate lectures without checking understanding, omits the medication history or fasting, lets him drive home, leaves out perforation or the alternatives, or does not document consent. In Part 2 they may call it ulcerative colitis, start mesalazine, or plan immunosuppression without screening.
explain:
Explaining a procedure: IPBRAD

Explanation and consent stations reward a structure. Start by asking what the patient knows, what they want to know and any previous experience. Then cover:

  • Indication: what the test is and why this patient needs it.
  • Procedure: before, during and after.
  • Benefits.
  • Risks, including the risk of not having it.
  • Alternatives.
  • Documentation: written information and signed consent.

Contraindications can be added where relevant. Check understanding throughout, avoid jargon, and remember that patients are often more anxious than they appear. Valid consent needs capacity, adequate information, voluntariness and the freedom to change one's mind. The ACSQHC Colonoscopy Clinical Care Standard expects informed decision-making supported by written information, appropriate bowel preparation and sedation, and discharge with information about what to expect and a follow-up plan.

Colonoscopy for Samuel

  • Indication: a thin, flexible tube with a camera passed through the anus to examine the colon and terminal ileum. It is used for screening and surveillance, bleeding, pain, altered bowel habit and IBD. In suspected Crohn's disease, ileocolonoscopy with biopsies is the first-line test.
  • Before: stop oral iron 5 to 7 days before, because it darkens and thickens the stool and impairs views. Stop loperamide (Gastro-Stop) a few days before the prep, as the unit instructs. Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are managed according to the unit's instructions. Low-fibre diet, then clear fluids the day before. The bowel prep, often split between the evening before and the morning of the procedure, causes frequent watery stools, so stay near a toilet and keep drinking. Fast before sedation as the unit instructs, because sedation needs an empty stomach to reduce the risk of aspiration.
  • During: a day procedure of about 20 to 30 minutes under sedation through a drip, usually given by an anaesthetist; most people are asleep or very drowsy and do not remember it, though it is not a full general anaesthetic. The doctor looks for inflammation, ulcers, polyps, masses and bleeding, takes biopsies and removes polyps.
  • After: recovery for a few hours, then home. No driving, operating machinery, alcohol or legal decisions for 24 hours. A responsible adult takes the patient home and ideally stays overnight. Bloating and cramps from the air settle quickly.
  • Benefits: a definite diagnosis with tissue, and early, appropriate treatment.
  • Risks: bloating and discomfort; reactions to the bowel prep (nausea, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance); reactions to sedation; bleeding (about 1 in 100 to 1,000 after polyp removal); infection; perforation (about 1 in 1,000 to 3,000, higher with polyp removal or severe inflammation), which is serious and may need surgery; and missed lesions. Not having the test risks missing Crohn's disease and letting it progress to strictures, fistulas and malnutrition.
  • Contraindications: known or suspected perforation, inability to tolerate sedation, pregnancy (relative), acute diverticulitis and fulminant colitis.
  • Alternatives: CT or MR enterography, flexible sigmoidoscopy (left colon only), capsule endoscopy (no biopsy, and a retention risk if there is a stricture) and barium enema (historical). Colonoscopy is the most accurate test for suspected IBD and the only routine test that lets the whole colon and terminal ileum be seen and biopsied.

Interpreting the results

  • Colonoscopy: deep linear ulcers and cobblestoning (ulcers separating islands of oedematous mucosa) in the terminal ileum, patchy disease with normal mucosa in between (skip lesions), and rectal sparing are the endoscopic hallmarks of Crohn's disease. Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum, and any ileal change is limited to mild backwash ileitis. A perianal skin tag, as Samuel has, also fits Crohn's disease.
  • Histology: chronic architectural distortion means long-standing inflammation. Patchy focal active colitis with normal mucosa between affected areas fits Crohn's disease, whereas ulcerative colitis gives diffuse, continuous changes. Non-caseating granulomas support Crohn's disease, although they are found in only a minority of biopsies. Caseation or acid-fast bacilli would suggest intestinal TB, an important mimic of ileocaecal Crohn's disease, especially before anti-TNF therapy.
  • Bloods: ferritin rises with inflammation, so a low ferritin during active disease confirms iron deficiency. With inflammation, iron deficiency can still be present at a ferritin up to about 100. Raised CRP and platelets with a low albumin mark active disease. Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease unlikely while the patient is eating gluten. Terminal ileal disease can cause B12 deficiency.
  • Stool: a raised calprotectin separates inflammatory from functional disease. The stool pathogen PCR, including Yersinia, a cause of ileitis, and C. difficile testing exclude infection.

Management (eTG Gastrointestinal: inflammatory bowel disease)

  • Induction: corticosteroids. Budesonide 9 mg orally daily for about 8 weeks, then tapered, suits mild to moderate ileocaecal disease. Prednisolone (for example 40 mg orally daily, tapering over about 8 weeks) is used for more severe disease, with calcium and vitamin D while on prednisolone. Steroids are not used for maintenance. Mesalazine is not used for induction; aminosalicylates have little role in Crohn's disease.
  • Maintenance: a thiopurine (azathioprine after TPMT, ± NUDT15, testing) or methotrexate. High-risk features favour earlier advanced therapy (anti-TNF and other biologics): young age at diagnosis, deep ulcers, extensive or small bowel disease, stricturing, perianal disease and smoking. For PBS-subsidised biologic therapy, the patient must have failed a tapered course of corticosteroids starting at prednisolone 40 mg daily or more (or equivalent) over 6 weeks, and 3 months or more of azathioprine (2 mg/kg daily or more), mercaptopurine (1 mg/kg daily or more) or methotrexate (15 mg weekly or more), unless contraindicated or not tolerated. They also need a CDAI of 300 or more, or alternative criteria (extensive small bowel disease of more than 50 cm, short gut syndrome, or an ileostomy or colostomy). Earlier use outside these criteria needs specialist advocacy or a trial.
  • Before immunosuppression: screen for hepatitis B and C, HIV, latent TB (IGRA and chest X-ray) and varicella immunity, and update vaccinations. Check EBV serology before a thiopurine, because a first EBV infection while on a thiopurine carries a risk of serious complications, including lymphoproliferative disease (ECCO). Avoid live vaccines once immunosuppressed.
  • Staging: MR enterography for small bowel extent and strictures. Pelvic MRI if perianal fistulising disease is suspected.
  • Supportive care: IV iron when the disease is active or oral iron fails. Ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphataemia; check phosphate if repeated doses are needed. Nutrition review; and smoking cessation, the most important modifiable factor in Crohn's disease. Involve the IBD nurse, dietitian, GP and psychological support.

Safety netting

After colonoscopy, severe or worsening abdominal pain, abdominal distension, fever, more than a small amount of rectal bleeding or vomiting need urgent review, because of the risk of perforation or bleeding. With Crohn's disease, obstructive symptoms (pain, vomiting, distension, not passing wind), fever, worsening or bloody diarrhoea, dehydration and perianal pain or swelling need same-day review through the IBD nurse or the ED. On immunosuppression, fever needs prompt assessment. Follow-up is in the IBD clinic with repeat bloods, calprotectin and the staging scan.
points: Structure a procedure explanation with IPBRAD: indication, procedure (before, during, after), benefits, risks including the risk of not having it, alternatives, and documentation. Find out what the patient knows first and check understanding throughout.

Before colonoscopy: stop oral iron 5 to 7 days beforehand and antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide a few days before the prep, manage anticoagulants as instructed, use a low-fibre diet then clear fluids and bowel prep, and fast before sedation. After sedation: no driving, alcohol or legal decisions for 24 hours, and a responsible adult takes the patient home.

Name the serious risks with approximate figures (perforation about 1 in 1,000 to 3,000; bleeding about 1 in 100 to 1,000 after polyp removal). Colonoscopy is the most accurate test for suspected IBD and the only routine test that lets the whole colon and terminal ileum be seen and biopsied.

Crohn's disease at colonoscopy: terminal ileal involvement, deep linear ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions and rectal sparing, with non-caseating granulomas on histology. Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum.
A low ferritin during active inflammation confirms iron deficiency. IV iron is preferred in active IBD.

Induce remission with corticosteroids (budesonide for mild to moderate ileocaecal disease), not mesalazine; plan steroid-sparing maintenance within PBS criteria, screen for hepatitis B and C, HIV, TB and varicella before immunosuppression, and support smoking cessation.
